evidence: The LC records identify two people: n50017941 is John Whitney Hall (1916-1997), author of Government and Local Power in Japan; n78017260 is John Ross Hall (born 1946), sociologist and author of The Ways Out, Gone from the Promised Land and Cultures of Inquiry. These are distinct authorities, not duplicate records. The 1932 credit under b is anomalous.

LC n82050699 identifies the historian John Brewer, author of Party Ideology and Popular Politics and The Sinews of Power. LC n78026200 identifies John David Brewer (born 1951), Belfast sociologist and author of Mosley's Men and Ethnography. The authorities represent distinct careers and people.

a combines John E. Smith's Time and Qualitative Time (publisher's 1986 contents) with Brendan Smith's Armagh-Clogher Dispute (Bristol research record), despite its Paul label. b's Loyalists and Redcoats and Letters of Delegates to Congress belong to Paul Hubert Smith. a is an aggregate of different authors, not a coherent Paul Hubert Smith bibliography.

LC n79061180 is Joseph Priestley (1733-1804), whose electricity, gases and Unitarian writings appear under a. LC n79116394 is John Boynton Priestley (1894-1984), whose novels and plays, including The Good Companions and Dangerous Corner, appear under b. The authority records describe different people born 161 years apart.

a conflates at least Jonathan Alexander, credited by The Art Bulletin with Labeur and Paresse, and Jocelyn Alexander, credited with The Local State in Post-War Mozambique. Neither attribution identifies Jeffrey C. Alexander, whose Theoretical Logic in Sociology and The Civil Sphere form b's sociological-theory career.

a's sole item is Eric Ledell Smith's edition of historical correspondence, not an established modern publication by John Henderson. LSU's Joseph Watson finding aid identifies John Henderson as a participant in recovering kidnapped children in 1827. b is LSU's modern Chinese intellectual historian John B. Henderson, whose faculty bibliography lists all four supplied books.

LC n83227286 identifies John Elgin Foster through The Developing West, matching a's Canadian West and buffalo history. LC n88204101 identifies John Foster (born 1940), professor at Paisley and author of The Politics of the UCS Work-In; his Class Struggle and the Industrial Revolution belongs to the same British labour-history career. These are distinct authorities and people.

LC n86120217 identifies Andrew Christian Ross (1931-2008), Edinburgh divinity dean and author of John Philip and Colonialism to Cabinet Crisis. LC n88109945 identifies Andrew Ross (born 1956), NYU cultural analyst and author of The Failure of Modernism and Microphone Fiends. Their mission-history and cultural/labour studies bibliographies belong to different people.

a mixes Robert G. Evans's health-economics article Fee Controls as Cost Control, Richard J. Evans's Roman consular-election study, and R. J. W. Evans's Habsburg lecture Communicating Empire. These are different authors, not one Raymond Evans bibliography. b's books concern Queensland race relations and Australian history.

The publisher credits A Military Strength Report from Vindolanda to J. David Thomas of Durham, matching a's other Roman papyrology papers. a also includes James E. Thomas's 1929 Cornish Carols credit, so the initial-only key is mixed. b is Julian Thomas, whose supplied books concern Neolithic and landscape archaeology, not these authors.

LC n80045215 identifies John Joseph Collins (born 1946), the Yale biblical scholar behind a's Sibylline Oracles and apocalypticism books. LC n91091136 identifies Edmund John Collins (born 1944), Ghanaian-music scholar behind b's West African Pop Roots. a also contains the latter's The Early History of West African Highlife Music and Jazz Feedback to Africa: it mixes these distinct people.

LC n97102565 identifies Robert W. Jones (born 1969), the Leeds eighteenth-century specialist behind Gender and the Formation of Taste and the Sheridan studies. LC n83064538 identifies Robert Tudur Jones (1921-1998), Welsh church historian behind The Great Reformation and Ffydd ac Argyfwng Cenedl. These are distinct people; a's 1903 medical article is an additional misattribution.

Cambridge credits a's only article, Asquith's Choice, to R. J. Q. Adams, the historian of British politics and conscription. b's Protests by Pupils, Social Work and Empowerment and subsequent social-work textbooks belong to Robert Adams (born 1944). The expanded article byline resolves the ambiguous initial and does not match b.

LC n84013904 is David Graham Bell (born 1953), the New Brunswick legal historian behind a's Loyalist books; n83040587 is David Neil Bell (1943-2025), the medieval theologian behind b's The Image and Likeness. a includes the latter's The Tripartite Soul and the Image of God, alongside French-history and physics credits. The authorities are distinct, but a conflates multiple people including b.

LC nb96009926 identifies David Green (born 1969), medieval historian at Harlaxton and author of The Black Prince. LC n50033951 identifies David Bronte Green (born 1910), author of Grinling Gibbons, Blenheim Palace and Gardener to Queen Anne. The authorities describe different people. a's unrelated economics and wealth-history articles do not connect these two careers.
